title: Real, Pretend, or Changed?
tagline: Young detectives move, wiggle, or freeze to decide whether a picture or story is real, pretend on purpose, or changed to look real, and learn to ask a grown-up when they can't tell.
groupSize: Whole class with movement, then pairs; any class size
overview: Pretend is wonderful. Stories, cartoons, and drawings are made up on purpose, and everyone knows it. The tricky kind is a picture that has been **changed**, or made by a computer, so it *looks* real. In this game, you describe pictures and stories aloud, and children stand tall for **Real**, wiggle for **Pretend**, or freeze like a statue for **Changed**. They practice three detective questions and learn the most important move of all: when you can't tell by looking, ask a grown-up and check.
objectives: Students will sort described pictures and stories into real, pretend on purpose, and changed or computer-made, and give a clue for one choice.
Students will use detective questions (Could this really happen? Who made it? Does something look strange?) to explain their thinking to a partner.
Students will explain that computers can now make pictures that look like real photos, so looking alone is not always enough.
Students will name a grown-up they can ask to help check.

print: Handout A: Real, Pretend, or Changed? sort strips (1 teacher set, cut apart)
Handout B: Clue Detective Checklist (1 per pair, or 1 enlarged for the board)
Handout C: My Detective Page (1 per student)
Three signs on the board or wall: REAL (stand tall), PRETEND (wiggle), CHANGED (freeze); crayons
digital: Optional: an AI image generator your district approves, run by the teacher on a projector
Optional: a real photo you took of your classroom or playground, shown on the projector

prep: Cut apart the 12 strips from Handout A. Put them in the order listed; the first four are the easiest.
Post the three signs with a stick-figure pose drawn next to each.
Print or enlarge Handout B so the three detective questions are visible to everyone.
If you'll do the projected demo, try your district-approved image generator ahead of time with the prompt in the Digital section, and take one real photo of your classroom.

steps.title: "I saw a dog as tall as a house!"
steps.body: Say with great excitement: **"On my way to school I saw a dog as tall as a house!"** Pause. Ask: "Do you believe me? Thumbs up or thumbs down." Then: "What if I showed you a picture of it? Would you believe it then?" Let children talk. Say: "Today you're detectives. Some things are real, some are pretend, and some are changed to trick our eyes."
steps.note: Many children will say a picture would prove it. Hold on to that; the lesson will show that pictures can be changed.

steps.title: Three kinds, three poses, three questions
steps.body: Teach the poses: **REAL** means it really happened or really exists (stand tall). **PRETEND** means made up on purpose, like a story or a cartoon, and that's OK (wiggle). **CHANGED** means someone changed a real picture, or a computer made it, so it *looks* real but isn't (freeze like a statue). Then read the three detective questions on Handout B aloud: "Could this really happen? Who made it? Does something look strange?" Model one strip, thinking aloud with all three questions.
steps.note: The key difference between pretend and changed: pretend doesn't try to fool you. Changed does, or at least it looks real when it isn't.

steps.title: Detective moves
steps.body: Read each strip aloud, slowly. Children show the pose. Pick one child: **"What clue helped you?"** Then tape the strip under the matching sign. Every third strip, have partners turn and tell each other their clue using the frame: "I think it's ___ because ___." For strips like the lion in the kitchen, ask: "If you really weren't sure, who could you ask?"
steps.note: Expect disagreement on some strips. That's healthy. Ask both sides for their clue and remind them that detectives explain their thinking.

steps.title: How does a picture get changed?
steps.body: Hold up a child's drawing (with permission) or a simple drawing you made of a house. Say: "This is a real drawing of my house." Tape a paper cut-out of a giant cat on the roof. "Now it's changed. If I took a photo of it, would it look real?" Then explain simply: **"Some computers use AI to make pictures. You type words, and the computer makes a picture that can look just like a real photo. So sometimes our eyes can't tell. That's why we ask a grown-up and check."**
steps.note: Avoid telling children they can always spot fakes by looking for extra fingers or blurry spots. Those clues sometimes help, but computer-made pictures keep getting better. Checking with a trusted grown-up and a trusted source is the lasting habit.

steps.title: My Detective Page
steps.body: Children complete Handout C: draw something real, something pretend, and something that could be changed, then name a grown-up to ask. Pairs share one drawing with each other using the frame "This is ___ because ___." Invite two pairs to share with the class.
steps.note: Listen for reasons, not just labels. "It's changed because fish can't skateboard and it looks like a photo" is strong evidence.

unplugged: The entire lesson works with the printed strips, your voice, and the paper cut-out demonstration. The paper "change a picture" move in the Explore step shows children how editing works without a screen.
digital: In the Explore step, project a real photo you took of your classroom and let children name what they recognize. Then, as the class watches, type into a district-approved AI image generator: "A realistic photo of a dog as tall as a house, standing next to a car." Show the result beside your real photo and ask: "Which one is real? How can we tell? Could we tell if we didn't know?" Children never use the image tool themselves; you drive it on the projector.
whyTech: The sort and poses work best unplugged. The projected demo earns its few minutes: seeing a computer make a realistic picture from words, right beside a real classroom photo, shows children why "it has a picture" is not proof, which a description alone cannot do.

adaptations.label: Kindergarten
adaptations.text: Start with only REAL and PRETEND for the first six strips, then add CHANGED with the paper cut-out demo.

adaptations.label: Grade 2
adaptations.text: Pairs write a short "changed" caption for a real classroom photo (for example, "Our class pet is a baby dragon") and explain how a reader could check it.

adaptations.label: Emergent bilinguals
adaptations.text: The poses carry meaning without words. Add simple sketches to the strips and teach "real," "pretend," and "changed" in both languages.

adaptations.label: Children who can't move freely
adaptations.text: Use three colored cards (green for real, yellow for pretend, blue for changed) instead of poses.

lookFors: Children give a clue for their choice ("lions don't live in kitchens," "it's a storybook"), not just a label.
Children tell pretend apart from changed by asking whether it is trying to look real.
During the demo or reflection, children say that a picture can look real and still be made by a computer, and name a grown-up to ask.
reflection: How can you tell if a picture is real? What if you can't tell by looking?
Do I stay safe and make good choices when I use the internet? (Student ELE guiding question)
Why is pretend OK in a storybook but tricky in a photo?
transfer: Invite families to play "Real, Pretend, or Changed?" with pictures they see together in books, on cereal boxes, or on a screen, asking the three detective questions. Next lesson, *Ask Two* adds the habit of checking what a computer tells us with a second source.

handouts.title: Real, Pretend, or Changed?
handouts.instructions: Teacher: read each strip aloud. Children show the pose. Tape the strip under the sign.

items.text: A photo of a giraffe at the zoo, eating leaves from a tall tree.
items.why: Giraffes really eat leaves from tall trees. Nothing looks strange.

items.text: A storybook page: a bear rides a bicycle to the library.
items.why: A storybook is made up on purpose. That's OK!

items.text: A photo of a dog as tall as a house, standing next to a car.
items.why: Dogs can't be that big, but it looks like a real photo.

items.text: A photo of our school playground with snow on the slide. Our teacher took it last winter.
items.why: We know who made it and it could really happen.

items.text: A cartoon about a pumpkin that tells jokes.
A photo of a family picnic, but the sky is purple and there are two suns.
items.why: Our sky has one sun. Someone changed it or a computer made it.

items.text: A drawing a classmate made of a unicorn.
items.why: Unicorns are pretend, and a drawing isn't trying to trick us.

items.text: A video of firefighters spraying water on a fire, from a TV news show.
items.why: Firefighters really do this, and news shows tell us who made the video.

items.text: A picture that looks just like a real photo: a fish riding a skateboard.
items.why: Fish can't skateboard. It looks real, so it was changed or computer-made.

items.text: A photo of the moon at night, taken from a backyard.
items.why: You can see the moon from your backyard.

items.text: A photo of a boy standing next to a lion in his kitchen.
items.why: Lions don't live in kitchens. If you're not sure, ask a grown-up.

items.text: A puppet show where a sock puppet sings a song.
items.why: Everyone knows it's a puppet. It's pretend on purpose.

handouts.title: Clue Detective Checklist
handouts.instructions: Use these questions like a detective. Check each one you asked.
items: I asked: Could this really happen?
I asked: Is it pretend on purpose, like a story or cartoon?
I looked: Does something look strange or not quite right?
I remembered: A computer can make pictures that look real.
I asked a grown-up to help me check.

handouts.title: My Detective Page
handouts.instructions: Draw in each box. Your teacher can help with words.

sections.prompt: Draw a picture that could be CHANGED to trick someone.
If I can't tell, I will ask: ___
